clips.text_zh: 又見 /biz/ 膠膠噏：BTC 靜咗幾星期 大家都唔理 一升15%就個個衝入去。why buy after the move? 真係FOMO到癲。我自己prop firm CFD都未止血 睇到呢d post 更加諗多咗 🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Why buy BTC after the pump? You watch BTC do nothing for weeks and ignore it completely. Then it pumps 15% and suddenly everyone wants in. Why does everyone want to buy after the move already happened? This thread on /biz/ is calling out the classic FOMO pattern. The post is dated September 3, 2026.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ rant about FOMOing into BTC after a 15% pump

signal.rationale: Post-hoc FOMO observation, no actionable setup, OP just questions the crowd

clips.text_en_b2: The whole /biz/ thread is pointing out a textbook FOMO trap in the BTC market. For weeks the price flatlines and nobody pays the slightest attention; then a 15% pump kicks in and suddenly everyone piles in. The underlying logic, which the post highlights rather effectively, is that buying after the move has already happened makes little sense. Thread dated September 3, 2026.
clips.text_en_c1: The eternal question, restated for anyone who trades crypto: why on earth would you pile into BTC after the move has already happened? The pattern is depressingly predictable. Weeks of sideways action, complete indifference from the retail crowd, and then the moment a 15% rally materialises, everyone scrambles to buy at the very level they should have been accumulating weeks earlier. A /biz/ thread from September 3, 2026, lays out this textbook FOMO cycle with characteristic disdain. It is the sort of post that makes you reconsider your own risk management, particularly when your prop firm CFD positions remain stubbornly in the red.
clips.text_en_c2: The question posed on /biz/ cuts to the heart of a recurring pathology among retail participants: why on earth would anyone chase an asset immediately after it has already moved fifteen percent? For weeks Bitcoin idled in narrow ranges, drawing nothing but indifference from the very same crowd that now scrambles to establish exposure at the worst possible juncture. The thread, dated September 3, 2026, lays bare the mechanics of FOMO in clinical fashion, observing that buying the breakout after the impulse has already played out is, in effect, paying top dollar for momentum that has largely been spent. The underlying psychology is hardly novel.

clips.text_en_c2: A /biz/ compilation dated September 3, 2026 lays bare the fifteen-year performance gap with almost embarrassing clarity: a single thousand dollars deployed at the outset would have compounded into roughly 8.97 million in Bitcoin, 735,000 in Nvidia, 231,000 in Tesla, 29,000 in Apple, 8,400 in the S&P 500, and a comparatively paltry 2,150 in gold. The thread implicitly indicts risk-averse orthodoxies that dismissed the asset class at every stage.

clips.text_en_c1: OpenAI has formally unveiled GPT-6 Astra, and the company is wasting no time with corporate understatement, declaring outright that we have entered the AGI era. Internal benchmarks lend substantial credibility to that claim, with the model reportedly nearing saturation on the notoriously demanding ARC AGI 3 evaluation. The announcement, dated September 3, 2026, has been treated by /g/ as a genuine inflection point rather than mere marketing hyperbole, though seasoned observers remain understandably sceptical. Whether this constitutes genuine artificial general intelligence or simply another incremental leap in capability is, of course, a matter of considerable debate.
clips.text_en_c2: OpenAI's unveiling of GPT-6 Astra, accompanied by the scarcely understated declaration that we have entered the AGI era, has predictably set /g/ ablaze. The company frames the model as its most capable and best-aligned release to date, and the benchmarks lend at least superficial credence to that claim: the system nearly saturates ARC-AGI-3, a suite previously regarded as a credible frontier for measuring general reasoning. Whether saturation constitutes genuine intelligence or merely the exploitation of patterns embedded in test design remains, of course, a separate and considerably thornier question. The September 3, 2026 announcement has nonetheless been received, in characteristic fashion, as the long-anticipated inflection point at which artificial intelligence decisively outpaces whatever professional competencies its users happen to possess.

clips.text_en_c2: In a thread dated September 3, 2026, a /pol/ poster offers the geopolitical prescription that, once China assumes dominion over New Zealand, the authorities should forthwith proscribe the haka, which he deems the most excruciating cultural spectacle ever to emanate from that corner of the globe. It is, in essence, rhetorical performance calibrated less for persuasion than for the approbation of those already convinced.

clips.text_en_c2: A /v/ thread from September 3, 2026 celebrates what its participants regard as a delicious inversion of the Japanese PC gaming hierarchy: an eroge has seized the number-one position on Steam Japan, outselling every Western AAA title currently available in that market. The irony is hardly subtle. A niche adult visual novel, produced for a comparatively minuscule audience, has eclipsed blockbusters commanding nine-figure marketing budgets and decades of institutional prestige. The thread savors the absurdity with considerable relish, framing the result as a quiet vindication of domestic Japanese game design sensibilities that Western publishers, with their relentless homogenization, have conspicuously failed to anticipate. clips.text_zh: /fit/ 條post笑死：cut緊所以bench跌 膊頭痛所以唔squat 換grip所以bench跌45lbs。全部都係藉口lol。我自己160lbs cut緊 睇到好有共鳴 🙏
clips.text_en_b1: I'm cutting, that's why my bench is going down. My shoulders are bad, that's why I don't squat anymore. I started benching with a narrower grip, so my bench dropped 45lbs. The /fit/ poster lists every classic excuse one after another, posted on September 3, 2026.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread parodying the chain of cutting excuses lifters give
clips.text_en_b2: The /fit/ post strings together every classic lifting excuse in the book, and the result is pretty funny. The poster blames his ongoing cut for a bench plateau, dodges squats because his shoulders hurt, and then somehow lost 45 pounds off his bench after switching to a narrower grip. Each excuse on its own is familiar, but stacked together the pattern is unmistakable. Thread posted September 3, 2026.
clips.text_en_c1: A /fit/ poster has compiled what can only be described as a definitive taxonomy of lifting excuses, and the result is uncomfortably relatable for anyone who has ever found themselves rationalising a stalled progression. Currently cutting, so the bench press is naturally in decline. Shoulders acting up, which conveniently explains the absence of any squatting from the programme. Switching to a narrower grip on bench, predictably resulting in a precipitous forty-five-pound drop in working weight. Each excuse, taken individually, might carry some merit; stacked together, they form an airtight alibi for any lifter whose numbers are heading in the wrong direction.
clips.text_en_c2: A /fit/ poster, posting on September 3, 2026, composes what amounts to a hymn of self-deception, cataloguing every rationalization a lifter might invoke to explain deteriorating performance: caloric deficit explains the flagging bench, shoulder discomfort excuses the abandoned squat, and a newly adopted narrower grip conveniently accounts for a precipitous forty-five-pound regression in pressing strength. Each excuse, taken individually, possesses a veneer of plausibility; collectively, they form an almost comic edifice of motivated reasoning. The thread functions less as confession than as communal recognition, since every reader who has ever endured a cut has constructed comparable alibis. The underlying truth, of course, is rather more pedestrian: a sustained deficit exacts a predictable toll on output, and no contortion of technique will alter that physiological reality.

clips.text_en_c1: A newcomer to Demon Slayer, currently making their way through the second season, has taken to /a/ to pose a question that has presumably nagged at countless viewers before them: why does the anime attract such disproportionate disdain from the broader community? The poster's central argument, posted on September 3, 2026, is that virtually every criticism levelled at the series applies with equal force to numerous other widely celebrated titles, suggesting that Demon Slayer's unpopularity stems less from any genuine failing than from the simple crime of having become too commercially successful for its own good.
clips.text_en_c2: An /a/ viewer, posting on September 3, 2026 while working through Demon Slayer's second season for the first time, poses the inevitable question: why does the series attract such disproportionate contempt from the very community ostensibly devoted to anime? He observes, with some justification, that every criticism routinely levelled at the show applies with equal or greater force to titles the same critics hold in high regard. The implication is that Demon Slayer is punished not for any aesthetic deficiency but for the unforgivable sin of being enormously popular. Such a diagnosis, while perhaps overly generous to the work itself, captures a recurrent pathology within fan communities, in which consensus taste instinctively recoils from any property that succeeds too emphatically with audiences deemed insufficiently discerning. It is contempt by proxy.
